subject: Scoring the general factor in a bifactor model

messages.author: 7de23bc44aa9ce1e
messages.subject: Scoring the general factor in a bifactor model
parts:
Hi Phil,

I am interested in scoring the general trait of the bifactor model in the simplest possible way (preferably so that it can be used by clinicians with limited statistical knowledge). I recently read the paper 'DeMars 2013: A Tutorial on Interpreting Bifactor Model Scores' and my interpretation is that once controlling for the specific factors, the coefficients from the general factor can be used independently to create the score. This confuses me since the bifactor model is compensatory in nature.

What is your opinion?

Best,
Rico


"In some contexts, the bifactor model may be chosen because the user wants to
interpret the general trait scores, controlling for nuisance factors. For example,
on an attitude survey, the negatively worded items might load on a specific factor,
as in Kim and colleagues’ (2011) study of a Korean adaptation of measures of
adult attachment. For this type of use, trait score estimates on the general factor
will represent more pure measures of the trait of interest after controlling for
this negative-wording factor." DeMars 2013

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Scoring the general factor in a bifactor model
parts:
DeMars' interpretation is correct, and yes you should be able to use the scores from a bifactor model's general factor independently. The idea is that the specific factors act as a type of residual covariance, and after accounting for these redundancies any left over common variation must have been due to the general factor. Computing the factor scores also accounts for this residual dependency effect so long as the specific factors are jointly included during estimation. So, while you're correct that the traits are compensatory, so long as the factor score components are modeled jointly then the inflation that would have occurred without these specific factors (e.g., fitting a unidimensional model) will provide more 'purified' estimates of the dominant trait. HTH. 

Phil
